headings.title: Introduction and Principles of Infant Feeding in HIV
headings.content: Infant feeding in the context of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) presents a unique and delicate clinical challenge for healthcare providers, particularly in resource-limited settings like Nigeria. The fundamental dilemma lies in balancing the nutritional, immunological, and psychological benefits of breastfeeding against the significant risk of postnatal mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV. Historically, guidelines swung dramatically between strict avoidance of breastfeeding and unrestricted nursing. Today, contemporary nursing care revolves around the principle of maximizing HIV-free survival for the infant while protecting maternal health. MTCT can occur during pregnancy, labor, delivery, or through breast milk during the postnatal period. Without interventions, the risk of transmission via breastfeeding ranges between 15% and 20%. Therefore, nursing students must understand that infant feeding counseling is never a one-size-fits-all approach. It requires a thorough understanding of viral load suppression, antiretroviral therapy (ART) adherence, and socio-economic realities of the mother. Nurses serve as frontline educators who must dispel cultural myths, provide non-judgmental support, and guide mothers to make informed, safe feeding choices. The ultimate goal is to eliminate vertical transmission while ensuring the infant achieves optimal growth and development, preventing malnutrition, stunting, and other fatal childhood illnesses that often accompany improper feeding practices.

headings.title: World Health Organization Guidelines on Infant Feeding
headings.content: The World Health Organization (WHO) provides global guidelines that shape national policies on infant feeding for mothers living with HIV, including protocols adapted by the Federal Ministry of Health in Nigeria. According to current WHO recommendations, national authorities in each country must decide whether health systems will primarily promote and support exclusive breastfeeding with maternal antiretroviral therapy (ART) or avoid breastfeeding altogether using safe replacement feeding. This decision is based on population-level considerations of child mortality rates, the safety and availability of replacement feeding, and the local burden of infectious diseases such as diarrhea and pneumonia. In settings where infectious diseases and malnutrition are major causes of under-five mortality—which is common across many parts of Nigeria—national guidelines strongly recommend that mothers living with HIV breastfeed exclusively for the first six months of life, provided both mother and infant are adherent to antiretroviral interventions. Conversely, in settings where replacement feeding is safe, sustainable, and affordable, avoidance of all breastfeeding is recommended. As nursing professionals, it is imperative to align clinical practice with national policy guidelines while tailoring the delivery of education to each individual mother's circumstances, ensuring she understands the rationale behind the recommended feeding practice in her specific environment.

headings.title: Exclusive Breastfeeding and Maternal Antiretroviral Therapy
headings.content: Exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) means the infant receives only breast milk from his or her mother or a wet nurse, and no other liquids or solids, not even water, with the exception of drops or syrups consisting of vitamins, mineral supplements, or medicines. When combined with maternal adherence to lifelong antiretroviral therapy, EBF drastically reduces the risk of postnatal HIV transmission while providing unmatched immunological and nutritional benefits. Antiretroviral therapy works by suppressing the mother's viral load in both plasma and breast milk to undetectable levels, thereby minimizing the presence of the virus that the infant could ingest. Nursing students must emphasize to mothers that viral suppression is the shield that protects the baby. For EBF to be successful and safe, the mother must maintain strict, daily adherence to her ART regimen. Nurses must assess adherence barriers, such as pill fatigue, side effects, stigma, or financial constraints, and provide active counseling and support. Furthermore, infant prophylaxis—typically in the form of daily nevirapine or azidothymidine (AZT) syrup administered for the first six weeks of life or longer—acts as an additional layer of defense, neutralizing any viral particles that might cross the infant's mucosal barriers. EBF should continue for the first six months, after which nutritionally adequate and safe complementary foods should be introduced while breastfeeding continues up to 12 months or longer.

headings.title: Replacement Feeding: Safety and Preparation
headings.content: Replacement feeding refers to the process of feeding an infant who is receiving no breast milk with a diet that provides all the nutritional requirements the infant needs. For HIV-positive mothers who choose or qualify for replacement feeding, adherence to the AFASS criteria is vital. AFASS stands for Acceptable, Feasible, Affordable, Sustainable, and Safe. If even one of these criteria is missing, replacement feeding can lead to severe malnutrition, diarrheal disease, and death, which may pose a greater risk to the infant than HIV itself. 'Acceptable' means the mother perceives no cultural or social barrier to formula feeding. 'Feasible' implies she has the time, knowledge, and equipment to prepare it. 'Affordable' means she can procure sufficient formula without compromising household finances. 'Sustainable' means the supply is continuous for as long as the infant needs it. 'Safe' means the formula is correctly prepared and stored, utilizing clean water and hygienic utensils. Nursing education must focus heavily on practical preparation skills. Mothers must be taught rigorous hygiene standards, including proper handwashing, boiling and cooling water correctly, sterilizing feeding bottles and cups, and avoiding the use of feeding bottles with nipples where possible, as cups are much easier to clean and carry a lower risk of microbial contamination. Preparing feeds in advance should be strongly discouraged to prevent bacterial proliferation.

headings.title: Mixed Feeding Risks and Prevention
headings.content: Mixed feeding—defined as giving an infant both breast milk and other foods, liquids, or formula during the first six months of life—is strictly contraindicated for HIV-positive mothers. Nurses must understand and explain the pathophysiology behind why mixed feeding dramatically increases the risk of HIV transmission compared to exclusive breastfeeding. Introducing non-human milks, water, or early complementary foods causes micro-trauma, inflammation, and irritation to the delicate mucosal lining of the infant's immature gastrointestinal tract. This damaged gut barrier allows HIV present in breast milk to easily cross into the infant's bloodstream. Furthermore, early introduction of contaminated water or food items frequently introduces pathogens that cause severe diarrhea and systemic infections. These infections lead to further gut inflammation, compromising immune defenses and heightening the window of susceptibility. Prevention of mixed feeding requires intensive counseling during antenatal and postnatal visits. Healthcare providers must actively identify if a mother is supplementing with water, teas, or infant formulas, and provide empathetic counseling to correct these practices. Support systems involving partners and family members are also crucial, as societal pressure to give water or traditional concoctions is a major driver of mixed feeding in many communities. Nurses must empower mothers with culturally sensitive negotiation strategies to resist pressure to mix-feed.

headings.title: Transition to Complementary Foods
headings.content: Transition to complementary foods marks a critical milestone at six months of age for infants born to HIV-positive mothers who have been exclusively breastfed. At this juncture, breast milk alone can no longer meet the expanding nutritional and energy demands of the growing infant, making complementary feeding essential. However, this transition must be managed carefully to ensure nutritional adequacy, safety, and continued prevention of HIV transmission if breastfeeding is ongoing. Complementary foods should be thick, nutrient-dense, and prepared from local, affordable foodstuffs rich in iron, protein, and essential vitamins. Nurses must educate mothers on hygienic food preparation, safe storage, and proper handwashing before feeding, as infant vulnerability to waterborne and foodborne pathogens remains high. If breastfeeding continues past six months alongside complementary foods—as recommended in many breastfeeding-supportive national guidelines—the mother must maintain strict adherence to her ART to keep her viral load suppressed throughout the extended breastfeeding period. Breastfeeding should ideally continue up to 12 months or until a nutritionally adequate and safe diet without breast milk can be provided. Abrupt cessation of breastfeeding is discouraged, as it can cause psychological distress for the child and nutritional disruptions. Instead, when the time comes to wean, cessation should be gradual over a period of weeks, ensuring the infant is transitioned smoothly to safe alternative nutrient sources.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Counseling for HIV-Positive Mothers
headings.content: Nursing assessment and counseling are the bedrock of successful prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) programs. Nurses must conduct comprehensive, empathetic assessments during every clinical encounter with an HIV-positive mother, evaluating her viral load results, ART adherence patterns, psychological well-being, breast health status (screening for mastitis, cracked nipples, or abscesses), and infant growth milestones. Effective counseling must be built on trust, confidentiality, and respect for the mother's dignity. Stigma and discrimination remain major deterrents to healthcare engagement; therefore, nurses must maintain a supportive and non-judgmental attitude. Counseling sessions should be individualized, empowering the mother to make informed choices regarding infant feeding based on national guidelines and her personal context. Nurses should also assess household support systems, engaging partners or family members where appropriate with the mother's consent, as partner involvement greatly improves PMTCT outcomes. Furthermore, nurses must schedule routine infant HIV diagnostic testing—such as DNA PCR tests at specific age intervals (e.g., at 6 weeks or birth depending on local guidelines)—and counsel mothers on the interpretation of results. By combining rigorous clinical assessment with compassionate counseling, nurses play an irreplaceable role in keeping HIV-positive mothers healthy and ensuring their infants remain HIV-free and well-nourished.
